resources.string: No position fix: tropo and aurora need one

Is it worth getting on the air beyond the usual range? Tropospheric ducting is the main source of long VHF/UHF contacts; aurora and meteor showers open short paths (mostly for SSB and digital modes, sometimes FM).

Grey normal · cyan slightly enhanced · green super-refraction (longer range) · amber ducting likely (hundreds of km). From the weather forecast\'s temperature and humidity layers near the ground (Open-Meteo, position rounded to about 50 km); thin ducts near the ground are underestimated, so a calm, clear night after a warm day can be better than shown.
VHF aurora signals bounce off the auroral oval to the north: point the antenna north, expect a rough, buzzing sound (it suits CW and SSB better than FM). It needs Kp 5 or more at mid latitudes.
No major shower in the next six weeks.
Each meteor trail reflects 2 m signals for a fraction of a second up to a few seconds (“pings”), from about 800 to 2000 km away; the best hours are before dawn.
No pass above 20° in the next 12 hours.
Passes above 20° in the next 12 hours; PKT → Satellite passes tracks them with Doppler.

Pick the mode and Listen: the decoder finds the signal by itself anywhere in the audio (RTTY mark 600 to 2700 Hz, PSK31 300 to 2700 Hz). You answer on the frequency being received, or on 2125 Hz (RTTY) and 1000 Hz (PSK31) when nothing is. Long text goes out in several transmissions, because this radio stops each one at 30 seconds.

Everything the radio hears on this channel (up to %1$s s) is recorded and sent back a second after the other station stops, so they can check how they sound through you. With a callsign set, it adds your callsign in Morse to a replay at most every %2$s minutes. The radio\'s 30-second transmit limit caps each replay.
No recordings yet. Turn REC on; every reception on the channel is saved under Download/DMR/Audio/<channel>/.

Tune the BBS or node\'s channel, then connect. Each exchange takes a few seconds: every transmission starts with a 1.6-second tone and lost frames are sent again. Type a line and Send; most BBSs answer with a prompt, and B or BYE ends the session.

The Koch method: start with two characters at full speed and add one each time you copy a lesson with 90 %. Farnsworth spacing leaves longer gaps between characters while you learn; close it up as you improve. Sound plays on the phone, not on the air.
Hold the key for dahs, tap for dits; after a pause of a second and a half the decoder shows what you sent and your speed.
(not readable yet: keep dits short and dahs three times as long)

Record with the phone\'s microphone (Record, speak, Stop; up to 25 seconds, silence at the ends is trimmed). Listen plays it on the phone; Send transmits it on the current channel. With Morse ID on, your callsign follows in Morse on amateur channels.

Amateur rules ask for your callsign every ten minutes while you talk and at the end. The timer starts with your first transmission on an amateur channel after you last identified; when it runs out, the phone vibrates and reminds you as you key. A Morse ID (PKT, the keyer or after talking) restarts it, or tap I just identified after saying your callsign.
Nothing yet. Tune the M17 frequency (the channel or the VFO). A transmission is found from its sync and played on the phone\'s speaker.

Hold to talk sends your voice as M17, to everyone (@ALL), up to the transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission). A short tail follows the last word so the ending is not cut off. Your callsign is the one in APRS settings.
